heroLedePart1: Right after a diagnosis the hardest part isn’t the missing answers — it’s

heroLedePart2: That you have to see the diagnosis through yourself. That a doctor who knows

introTitle: Five things you don’t know to ask about — in the order you’ll need them.
introSub: This isn’t a feature list. It’s the path a family walks after a diagnosis — each stop tells you what exists and what to do with it.
step1Hook: Nobody tells you the diagnosis is yours to double-check
step1Title: First, make sure it’s really this disease — and this subtype.
step1LedeFdA: The doctor establishes whether the lesion involves one bone, several bones, or also the skin and hormones (McCune-Albright syndrome). In a typical picture the diagnosis is made clinically, after a staging evaluation of the whole body; a biopsy is needed in unusual or questionable cases.
step1LedeFdB: The gene change is present in only some cells, so a negative genetic test from blood does not close the matter.
step1LedeGenericPart1: Many rare diseases look like more common ones on a first pass. Before anyone proposes treatment, the diagnosis and subtype must be confirmed — often
step1LedeGenericPart2: and on imaging, not by one test in isolation.
step1AnchorQuote: “In Warsaw our son had a histopathology the guideline didn’t require — and got a wrong diagnosis. Only the CT in Olsztyn and the GNAS test settled it.”
step1CtaConfirm: What to confirm, and in what order
askNote: These questions come straight from the guidelines. They do not mean anything went wrong — they help you check whether the picture is complete.
askQ1: “How was the diagnosis made? Which type is it?”
askS1: In most cases, the diagnosis of FD/MAS can be made clinically after a complete staging evaluation for skeletal, endocrine, soft tissue and dermatologic features.
askQ2: “Is the diagnosis certain in our case — and if not, is a genetic test for the GNAS mutation worth doing?”
askS2: A genetic diagnosis is recommended where the diagnosis is in question. This especially applies to isolated/monostotic lesions in the skull…
askQ3: “What does a negative genetic test from blood mean?”
askS3: Use of blood for mutation analysis cannot exclude the diagnosis of monostotic FD, but a positive result is informative.
askQ4: “Did the evaluation also cover skin, hormones and soft tissue, or only bone?”
askS4: …a complete staging evaluation for skeletal, endocrine, soft tissue and dermatologic features.
askQ5: “Is this a single lesion or are there more — and does that change how the diagnosis is confirmed?”
askS5: Isolated monostotic bone lesions without accompanying skin or endocrine findings include a wide differential diagnosis and diagnostic uncertainty and usually require histological confirmation.
askQ6: “In what situations is a biopsy done?”
askS6: Biopsy with histological evaluation of suspected bone disease is usually only necessary in unusual or questionable cases, and/or if malignancy is suspected.
askSource: Quotations are from: Javaid MK et al., Best practice management guidelines for fibrous dysplasia/McCune-Albright syndrome, Orphanet J Rare Dis 2019;14:139 (PMID 31196103). The questions were written by the GeneQuest Foundation; the guideline authors have not reviewed or approved them.
step2Hook: Not every surgeon or endocrinologist knows this disease
step2Title: A handful of doctors truly know {{name}}. Find them.
step2LedePart1: In a rare disease the most valuable — and hardest to find — person is a doctor who
step2LedePart2: knows this condition. We show the
step2LedePart3: (from PubMed: whether they have published on it, co-authored studies, or led them) and family recommendations — sorted by distance from you.
step2AnchorQuote: “We found the best doctors by word of mouth and by chance at a check-up — not from a search engine. That’s why a parent can add a doctor here, with a note.”

step0Hook: And if no one knows yet what’s wrong?
step0PredxLedePart1: Sometimes the problem isn’t “I have a diagnosis, what now” but
step0PredxLedePart2: . The interview works iteratively: it takes a broad first pass, then — depending on your answers — can search the literature before asking the next question. The goal is not diagnostic: it’s
step0PredxLedePart3: — which leads to explore, which specialist to consider, what to ask — written up as a document to discuss with your doctor.
safetyBold: Everything here is a starting point for a conversation with your doctor — not a recommendation.
safetyBody: We show official guidelines plainly; “to consider” recommendations and AI drafts always carry a label, a rationale, and a “discuss with your doctor” note. Your doctor makes the decisions — we help you know what to ask.
summarySub: A longer text, written mostly for your doctor: a summary of the official guidelines and newer papers, prepared by AI, with the source next to every paragraph.
dataTitle: Doctors, clinical trials, therapies and foundations
unusualTitle: Your case doesn't fit this description?
unusualBody: An unusual course, results that contradict each other, or doctors who disagree — write to us. We read every message. We will try to point you to papers and doctors who have described similar cases, and help you put together questions for your doctor. We don't diagnose and we don't judge treatment — that stays with your doctor.
unusualNote: Your message goes to the GeneQuest Foundation's inbox ({{email}}). Please don't attach medical records or anything that identifies your child — a few sentences are enough to start.
